subject: Zero and one inflated beta regression

messages.author: f120a4140c97c18f
messages.subject: Zero and one inflated beta regression
parts:
Hi, I have a data set of discard ratios [0,1] (fisheries) that is zeros and ones inflated (see figure below for an example of observations of Sole (SOL), Lemon sole (LEM) and Cod (COD)). 
Originally, I applied the beta distribution in INLA, but the residual plot shows a clear pattern which I assume due to the zeros and ones that the beta distribution could not model (please see the figure on the left below)

 
In order to solve the residual pattern, I tried the hurdle model binomial-beta. Binomial distribution for 0 (no discard) and positive values (discards) and beta distribution conditional on the positive values only. However, the problem does not seem to be solved (please see figure below)


Thus, I hope someone in the group could help me out. 
1. Is there any recommendation to model the type of data that I have?
2. Could it be possible to do zero-and-one-inflated-beta regression in INLA?
3. Is there any other solution if zero-and-one-inflated-beta regression in INLA is not possible (i.e. mixture of models?)?

I appreciate any help or advice. Thank you!

messages.author: ee8358804ba614e0
messages.subject: Re: Zero and one inflated beta regression
parts:
You tend to get that type of residual patterns with zero-inflated models/data. What you should do is to calculate the mean and variance of the combined model (we called it a ZABE model; zero-altered beta)....and simulate 1000 data sets from such a distribution. And see whether the simulated data sets are comparable to your observed data set.

Alain Zuur

messages.author: ee8358804ba614e0
messages.subject: Re: Zero and one inflated beta regression
parts:
On Thursday, August 13, 2020 at 2:35:47 AM UTC+1, Anh T. Bui wrote:
Dear Alain, 

Thank you for your advice. Do you have any resources that I can refer to related to the ZABE model or any similar type of zero-alter model? I just found out that the ZEBA model is described in your book "Beginner’s Guide to Zero-Inflated Models with R" but I currently cannot afford the book.

I did a lot of googling. I used Ospina and Ferrari (2011) a lot. Just google  'Ospina and Ferrari (2011)' and you will come as the first link. The principle is the same as a hurdle model for a Poisson...or the Bernoulli + Gamma combination.
Besides, I would like to ask what I might do in case the simulated data sets are not comparable to my observed data set?
The observed data set also had a lot of ones in it so I am afraid the beta distribution might not be able to capture all of those ones.

You are not simulating from a beta model. You are simulating from a joint Bernoulli and beta model. A beta model will never simulate zeros. The Bernoulli will take care of that.

Alain

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Zero and one inflated beta regression
parts: On Thu, 13 Aug 2020 at 21:41, Alain Zuur <high...@highstat.com> wrote:

The observed data set also had a lot of ones in it so I am afraid the beta distribution might not be able to capture all of those ones.

You are not simulating from a beta model. You are simulating from a joint Bernoulli and beta model. A beta model will never simulate zeros. The Bernoulli will take care of that.

For these particular data, it's probably right that a combination of Bernoulli and Beta is needed. But in more general practice, 0 and 1 outcomes _can_ and do occur in what might otherwise be well approximated by a Beta distribution, due to basic rounding of the recorded measurements, or related discretisation effects, where the 0/1 variables should only really be _close_ to 0/1.  I've been working on a solution to that aspect of the problem (the traditional solutions to that problem can introduce large bias), and Haavard has just this week implemented an experimental version of that solution (I don't think it's even in the built package yet; and even then it should be treated as experimental until we've done more work and writing on it).

Finn
